Colorado just reset its AI law. Most owners missed it.

On May 14, Governor Polis signed SB 26-189. It rewrites Colorado's AI law and pushes the effective date to January 1, 2027 (per Consumer Finance Monitor, May 2026).

The new version is narrower. It drops the algorithmic-discrimination duty and focuses on disclosure: if you use automated tools to make consequential decisions in hiring, lending, housing, insurance, or healthcare, you owe people transparency about it.

Here's the part small businesses miss. "We don't build AI" doesn't get you out of it. If you use an AI hiring screen, an automated loan pre-check, or a tool that ranks patients, you're likely in scope.

You have until January to know where you stand. That's not much runway for a business that also has to, you know, run.

You just don't see it happening.

Two numbers from this month. 38% of employees admit feeding sensitive company data into AI tools to save time (per PagerDuty's 2026 shadow-AI survey). At companies under 10 people, 59% have no AI policy at all (Founder Reports, 2026).

That's not a tech problem. It's an exposure problem. Client records, vendor spreadsheets, HR files, quietly leaving through a browser tab nobody approved.

1. Ask each person which AI tools they use. You'll hear names you didn't authorize.
2. Check whether those tools train on your inputs. Free tiers usually do.
3. Write one page: what's allowed, what's never pasted, who to ask.
